newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila bankers not keen to revive volatility band.
newsitem.headline: Manila bankers not keen to revive volatility band.

text.p: The Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) is not likely to reimpose the 1.5 percent volatility band in the foreign exchange market, BAP president Deogracias Vistan said on Monday.
The BAP temporarily suspended the volatility band earlier in the day after the Central Bank suggested doing away with it to allow freer movement of the peso.
"It has been shelved," Vistan told reporters after meeting with bank treasurers to assess the situation in the peso-dollar market.
"We may consider the volatility band if there will be a rapid appreciation of the value of the peso that will be deterrent to exporters," he said.

The volatility band was imposed to discourage wild fluctuation in the exchange rate. The band meant that trading would be stopped for two hours if the rate fluctuated either way beyond 1.5 percent of the previous day' weighted average.
Until last week, the band set up in 1994 was never invoked as the peso barely moved against the dollar.
But last Friday, the band came into effect after the peso dropped 11.5 percent to 29.45 pesos per dollar.
The plunge came after the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, or the central bank, said it would allow the peso to move in a wider range, which meant an effective devaluation.

Because the band was exceeded in Friday's trading, the BAP suspended trading and said all deals outside the 1.5 percent band would not be included in the reference rate, which is the average of all deals done.
The BAP's decision to ignore the day's low and maintain the average at 26.40 pesos had posed a problem as bankers predicted repeated trading suspensions in the market.
Early on Monday before trading began, the BAP decided to suspend the volatility band.

Vistan, who is also the president of Solid Bank Corp, said he expected peso trading to remain abnormal this week, although the trading range might be wedged within 50 centavos below or above the Central Bank's selling rate of 29 pesos.
Trading in the foreign exchange market on Monday was light with turnover of only $30.50 million, much lower than the normal $200 million.
Done rates ranged from a high of 27.50 to a low of 29.75.
"This will definitely be here all of this week," he said when asked how long he expected the uneasiness in the peso to persist.
